01 — How the naming system works

Three genuinely different
directions.

Each direction has two names. The direction name (A, B, C + concept word) is the designer's internal reference — what the direction is conceptually. The vibe word that appears on the moodboard is the emotional register — what it feels like. These are different because the concept and the feeling are not always the same thing.

Direction name = what the designer calls it internally, the creative concept.
Vibe word = what appears on the moodboard image, the emotional output.

Example: Direction A is called "Sunny" because the concept is warmth and optimism. The vibe word is "Bloom" because the feeling it produces is growth, flourishing, aliveness — a child in full bloom. Same idea. Different angle.

The three directions are genuinely distinct — not colour variations of the same idea. Each has a completely different palette, typeface, illustration register, and emotional territory. A parent choosing between them would be making a meaningfully different decision each time.

The feeling
Warm, confident, joyful, rooted. The feeling of a sunny Indian morning — marigold garlands, yellow school bags, mustard fields, ripe mangoes. This is what childhood in India looks and feels like. It is immediately recognisable and emotionally resonant. Priya sees it and thinks: yes, this is for us.
Who it appeals to
Urban aspirational Indian mothers who want something that feels premium but also feels warm and culturally familiar. It works across gifting occasions — birthdays, Diwali, baby showers. It is also the most Instagram-friendly direction — the yellow palette photographs beautifully against neutral backgrounds and wooden floors.
The risk
If executed with insufficient quality, yellow can read as cheap or generic. The line between "warm and premium" and "loud and low-cost" is thin in this palette. The illustration quality and typography system must be strong enough to hold the premium positioning. The risk is execution, not direction.

Books & toys for little explorers · Ages 3–6
The feeling
Adventurous, mysterious, alive with possibility. The feeling of a forest at dusk — fireflies, tiger stripes, monsoon green, rustling leaves. This direction is inspired by India's natural world: Panchatantra animals, jungle stories, the richness of Indian biodiversity. It is the most original direction — nothing like it exists in the Indian children's market.
Who it appeals to
A specific kind of urban Indian parent who reads Ruskin Bond to their child, values sustainability, and wants something distinctive — not the mainstream choice. This parent is probably slightly older (32–40), has a design sensibility, and actively seeks out brands that feel curated and unconventional. A smaller market, but extremely loyal.
The risk
Dark backgrounds with young children's products create friction — the category default is light, bright, and accessible. A deep forest green palette may feel unfamiliar for a gifting product. Grandparents buying gifts would not reach for this. The brand would need to work harder to earn trust and might take longer to find its audience at scale.

Books & toys · A gift they'll remember · Ages 3–6
The feeling
Tender, loving, celebratory. The feeling of wrapping a gift in tissue paper, of a child's birthday morning, of a mother choosing something with care. This direction is gifting-first — rose pink and turmeric gold are the colours of celebration in India. It feels like a hug. It feels like a baby shower. It feels like love made visible.
Who it appeals to
The gifting buyer more than the everyday buyer. Priya buying for her niece's birthday, a colleague's new baby, a festive occasion. Also strongly appeals to grandmothers and aunts making gifting decisions. The colour palette reads as feminine — which limits the range of gifters but deepens the loyalty of those who love it. Maximum gifting occasion conversion.
The risk
The palette reads as gender-coded — pink and rose suggest "for girls" to many buyers, which immediately halves the perceived addressable market for toys. It also does not carry the Indian cultural specificity of Direction A — the palette is universal gifting rather than specifically Indian celebration. A beautiful direction that may narrow rather than expand the brand's reach.
05 — Direction comparison · choosing one

Three directions.
One decision.

Direction A
Sunny / Bloom
The most commercially confident direction. Warm Indian yellow. Maximum gifting range — works for boys, girls, birthdays, Diwali, baby showers. Most Instagram-friendly palette. Strong cultural resonance. Execution-dependent but highest reward if done well.
Direction B
Wild / Lush
The most original direction. Deep forest green, firefly yellow, tiger orange. Inspired by India's natural world. Distinctive and memorable — nothing like it exists in the market. Smaller initial audience but fiercely loyal. Higher friction for casual gifting buyers.
Direction C
Sweet / Petal
The strongest gifting direction. Rose pink, turmeric gold. Maximum emotional pull at the purchase moment. Gender-coded risk narrows the audience. Beautiful but less culturally specific to India. Best for gifting occasions, more limited for everyday purchase.
Recommended direction for Bumblebee World
Direction A — Sunny / Bloom. Warmth, cultural rootedness, and commercial confidence in one palette. It passes Priya's Instagram test, her gifting test, and her cultural pride test simultaneously. Choose A, then execute it with Usborne-level illustration quality.
